title: De altitudine columnarum sub proprio pondere corruentium

deep.reconstruction:
Context (E510, §§29–31). Euler models a uniform heavy column that stands vertically, is fixed at its base and free at its top, and is loaded only by its own weight. He asks for the height b at which the straight form first becomes unstable.

Measure x from the top and write s = x/b. The slope u = y' then satisfies an Airy-type equation u'' + (t/b^3)·x·u = 0, with t = b^3/m. Euler solves the problem with power series in t; the products 1·4·7… and 1·3·6… in the coefficients are the usual coefficients of Airy (Bessel-1/3) series.

The series and the eigenvalue equation:
- P is the integral of the even fundamental solution, evaluated at the base. Its coefficients check: 1·4/7! = 1/1260 = 1/(2·3·5·6·7).
- P', Q and Q' are the further integrals and companions needed to impose the end conditions.
- The previous page reduces the end conditions to a 2×2 determinant. After division by b² this gives the transcendental equation P + PQ' − QP' = 0 in the single absolute number t.

§30 (this page): Euler finishes listing Q and Q'. He says the root t can only be found by trial: take successive trial values and infer the true root from their errors, i.e. regula falsi / secant-type interpolation. He warns that t is 'not small but rather fairly large'. The next page builds logarithmic recursions for the terms, carried to 20 terms, for numerical summation.

§31: the result is turned into usable units by calibrating with a test column of the same material. That column has height a, cross-section dd, and is known by experiment to carry a load Γ = λ·(its own weight) = λ·a·dd (unit specific weight). From his earlier Euler-load theory (E508/E238 line), Γ = π²Ekk/a², and he writes Ekk = d⁴e. Hence e = Γa²/(π²d⁴) = λa³/(π²dd).

In modern terms the critical condition reads w b³/EI = t, with w = dd and EI = d⁴e. So b³ = dd·e·t, and substitution gives b³ = λa³t/π², i.e. b = a·∛(λt/π²). The printed final formula instead reads b = a∛(λbb/(ππdd)).

Scaling law: for fixed e, b ∝ (dd)^{1/3}, i.e. the critical height goes as the cube root of the cross-section. This is the 'ratio subtriplicata' cited on the previous page and matches the theorem appended to the preceding dissertation. The modern answer (Greenhill 1881) is t = wL³/EI ≈ 7.837, the first zero condition of J_{-1/3}(⅔√t).
errors: The final printed formula b = a∛(λbb/(ππdd)) cannot be right: it lacks the eigenvalue t and contains b on both sides. With b³ = dd·e·t (Ekk = d⁴e, weight per length dd) and e = λa³/(π²dd), the correct result is b = a∛(λt/π²). This is evidently a misprint, likely 'bb'/'dd' carried over from the line b = ∛(bbet) [read ddet] on the previous page.
On the previous page 'b = ∛(bbet)' should be ∛(ddet), with dd the cross-section; otherwise the subtriplicate law in the amplitude would not follow.

Euler's remark that t must be 'satis magnum', together with the 20-term log tables on the next page, suggests he expected a root much larger than the correct 7.837. The historical literature (Timoshenko, Truesdell) reports that Euler's treatment of the self-weight column did not reach the correct critical value, later found by Greenhill in 1881. I am unsure precisely where his error enters (formulation of the boundary conditions vs. numerics); this page alone cannot settle it.
In Q' the third denominator is printed '1……10' rather than '2……10'. This is numerically harmless, since 1·2·…·10 = 2·…·10.

ideas.what: Buckling of a heavy column under its own weight reduced to a transcendental equation in a dimensionless number t = w b³/EI, expressed by Airy/Bessel-type power series
ideas.modern_name: Greenhill's problem (self-weight buckling); Airy / Bessel J_{±1/3} eigenvalue condition
ideas.usually_credited_to: Greenhill 1881 (correct solution); Euler 1778 credited with the first attempt
ideas.where_published: E510 itself (Acta Acad. Sci. Petrop. 1778); companion papers E508, E509

ideas.what: Solving the transcendental equation by trial values and interpolating from their errors
Calibration of the elastic constant via an experimental test column carrying λ times its own weight, using the Euler load π²EI/a²
ideas.modern_name: dimensional scaling / similitude calibration of critical load

ideas.what: Critical height scales as the cube root of the cross-sectional area (for geometrically similar sections)
ideas.where_published: E510 / theorem appended to preceding paper (E509?)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a known, historically discussed page: Euler's series-based attempt at the self-weight column, a regula-falsi plan and a calibration via the Euler load. It contains only a misprint in the final formula and nothing absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: Q' third term: the image indeed shows '1……10'; it is equivalent to 2……10.
The final formula as printed is 'b = a∛(λbb/(ππdd))', which matches the transcription, but mathematically it should be b = a∛(λt/ππ).
Previous page 'hoc est t [?] = ∛(bbet)' should likely read 'b = ∛(ddet)'.
